- The Tigray conflict in Ethiopia has intensified with the entry of Eritrean soldiers into the region.
- The 2022 peace deal between the Ethiopian government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) has collapsed, with both sides accusing each other of violations.
- The TPLF, now allied with six other Ethiopian armed groups, recently seized the Tigray airport, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend operations there.
- Diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated, with Ethiopia closing its Asmara embassy and expelling Eritrean diplomats.
The Tigray conflict, which has typically been between the Ethiopian military and regional forces, recently saw the entry of soldiers from neighbouring Eritrea.
Reports indicate that Eritrean soldiers were spotted in the Northern region of Ethiopia, the hotspot for the civil war that has plagued the country for years.

Back in 2022, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Ethiopian government, after two years of a brutal war, decided to make peace.
However, fighting between the two parties resumed 2 weeks ago as they both point the finger at each other for violating the 2022 peace deal.
Following the escalation of tensions, the TPLF seized control of the airport in the Tigray region, which subsequently compelled Ethiopian Airlines, Africa's largest air carrier, to suspend its operations at the facility.
At the same time, the TPLF revealed that it had allied with six other armed groups across Ethiopia aimed at overthrowing Abiy's government.
A week later, relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea, which have not historically been rosy, soured even further as Ethiopia shut its embassy in Asmara and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats out of the country.
The diplomatic fallout followed reports of explosions in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital and the headquarters of the African Union.
Tensions have also drawn in Egypt and Sudan.
Addis Ababa has accused both countries, along with Eritrea, of backing the opposition coalition, which includes the Tigray People’s Liberation Front.
Ethiopia believes that Eritrea, alongside Egypt and Sudan, are supporting the TPLF, an allegation all three countries deny.
However, per a BBC report, Eritrean military forces, which previously acted as allies to the Ethiopian government during the 2020 Tigray conflict, have recently re-entered Ethiopian territory.
This is according to multiple sources who cited Eritrean soldiers from the border town of Zalambessa towards central Tigray.
"I saw about 40 trucks carrying soldiers. The convoy was moving south," one resident of Adigrat, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told BBC Tigrinya.
A second resident reported seeing troop movements, initially at night: "We have been seeing trucks with Eritrean registration plates passing through the city.
"Now this morning we witnessed around 20 to 30 large trucks heading toward Edaga Hamus."
Tigray war
The Tigray war began in November 2020 after tensions between the Ethiopian government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) escalated into open fighting.
The conflict quickly drew in other forces, including troops from Eritrea and Ethiopia’s Amhara region.
Fighting spread across Tigray and into neighbouring areas, forcing millions of people from their homes and disrupting access to food, healthcare and other basic services.
The war stemmed from a political dispute that had been building since Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power in 2018.
The TPLF had played a major role in Ethiopia’s politics for decades but saw its influence decline under Abiy’s government.
On November 2, 2022, they signed the Pretoria Agreement, which ended the main fighting and provided a framework for disarmament and restoring federal authority in Tigray.

articles.title: Fuel imports push Ghana’s trade surplus down by 70% - GBC Ghana Online
articles.summary: Fuel imports push Ghana’s trade surplus down by 70%  GBC Ghana Online
articles.full_text:
By Ashiadey Dotse
Ghana’s growing dependence on imported fuel has put pressure on the country’s trade position, with fuel and mineral products making up about 30% of total imports in the second quarter of 2026.
Data from the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) show that diesel was the country’s largest single import during the period, costing GH¢12.2 billion.
Super petrol imports also accounted for about GH¢8 billion.
The high cost of fuel imports contributed to a 47.5% increase in Ghana’s total import bill between the first and second quarters of the year.
The GSS said rising international fuel prices were a major factor behind the increase.
Overall import prices went up by 22.7%, while fuel import prices rose sharply by 54.1% during the quarter.
As a result, Ghana’s trade surplus dropped from GH¢46.1 billion in the first quarter to GH¢13.8 billion in the second quarter, representing a decline of 70.1%.
The GSS has also warned that Ghana’s strong trade surplus is largely being supported by high export prices, particularly gold, rather than significant increases in the volume of goods exported.
It said this makes the economy vulnerable to changes in global commodity prices.
The Statistical Service is therefore calling for greater efforts to diversify Ghana’s exports, increase local processing and create more value from locally produced goods.
It has also urged stronger implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), improved transport and border infrastructure, and better access to financing for exporters.
According to the GSS, strengthening domestic production while reducing dependence on a few major exports will be important to building a more resilient trade position.

articles.title: Minerals Council South Africa Unveils Mining Investment and Growth Strategy - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: Minerals Council South Africa Unveils Mining Investment and Growth Strategy - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
The Minerals Council South Africa has launched an Investment and Growth Strategy aimed at drawing further investment into exploration, new mines and existing operations, according to Mining Weekly. The strategy, presented by council president Paul Dunne on October 7, seeks to grow the sector, create employment and provide job security.
Dunne said that while recent announcements of mine extensions, new mines and feasibility progress by member companies were encouraging, most of the R70-billion in committed investments ready for implementation was directed at maintaining output at current levels.
He noted that despite South Africa's mineral endowment, mining expertise and established industrial capability, the sector has not performed in line with that potential. Production remains below levels reached more than two decades ago, exploration expenditure has fallen by 80% over the past two decades, and the country attracts less than 1% of global exploration capital despite holding one of the world's most attractive geological opportunities.
According to Dunne, these figures represent deferred investment, unrealised production, forgone economic activity and employment opportunities that never materialised. He said the encouraging signs from mine extensions, new mines and feasibility studies must be supported by an enabling environment that invites global investment in South African mining.
He identified infrastructure quality, permitting efficiency, regulatory predictability, energy supply reliability and the effectiveness of public institutions as the factors determining the degree to which conditions for capital-intensive investment exist. Dunne said the country's mining challenges are not caused by geology, resource quality or investor interest, and that South Africa is well positioned to participate in a global economy increasingly shaped by demand for minerals needed for industrial development, energy security, advanced manufacturing and technological innovation. He described the broader operating and regulatory environment's ability to convert that opportunity into investment as the most significant constraint.
The strategy indicates that sustained yearly growth of 3% in the mining sector could add an estimated R65-billion to South Africa's GDP and support between 50 000 and 100 000 additional jobs by 2035. It aims to build an evidence-based understanding of the factors constraining mining investment and growth and to identify interventions most likely to improve the sector's contribution to the economy.
Dunne said the process identified multiple mining-specific barriers across the investment and operating environment and provided the foundation for one of the council's most important strategic initiatives in recent years. Many barriers are systemic. During consultations, infrastructure constraints related to logistics, electricity and water were consistently raised as key challenges, along with concerns about crime and illegal mining affecting competitiveness and raising operating costs. Junior mining and exploration companies identified obstacles that negatively affect South Africa's ability to attract early-stage investment, and the need for policy and administrative certainty emerged as a recurring theme.
Dunne noted that many constraints affecting mining growth sit beyond the direct control of the Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources. He said the inclusion of mining as one of three priority sectors of the Government-Business Partnership is a critically important development, and that the partnership provides a mechanism to align government departments, regulators, State-owned entities and the private sector around clearly defined priorities with measurable outcomes. The department and the council share joint accountability for delivering the outcomes committed to under the strategy.
The first workstream agreed with the department focuses on reducing administrative bottlenecks affecting mining projects, with the objective of unlocking more than R50-billion in capital expenditure by February 2028. Dunne said the investment pipeline is noteworthy because it demonstrates that substantial opportunities already exist within existing company portfolios, including new investments and projects capable of expanding current operations and extending mine lives.
The second workstream will focus on identifying the industry's competitiveness gaps and developing an understanding of the reforms required to strengthen South Africa's position as a mining destination. Dunne added that mining jurisdictions increasingly compete on institutional performance, administrative efficiency and the quality of their investment environment.
The third workstream supports the department's national implementation of a transparent and efficient mining cadastre by March 2027, which is considered a fundamental requirement for a competitive exploration environment and mineral rights administration.
Dunne said South Africa's mineral endowment remains one of its greatest economic advantages, but whether that advantage translates into higher investment, stronger exports, improved competitiveness and greater employment will depend less on the quality of the resources than on the effectiveness of the systems surrounding them. He said the strategy has provided a clear diagnosis and action plan, and that the Government-Business Partnership offers the most immediate pathway to implementation.

articles.title: FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks Join Forces to Deliver Landmark Power Interconnector to Supply the DRC’s Copperbelt - Novus Press Bulletin
articles.summary: FIS-RDC, EnPower, Trafigura and Gridworks Join Forces to Deliver Landmark Power Interconnector to Supply the DRC’s Copperbelt  Novus Press Bulletin
articles.full_text:
A 700MW cross-border transmission line will bring affordable power to the DRC’s Copperbelt, unlock new mining and industrial capacity, open export routes for licensed Zambian power producers, and enable new generation
KINSHASA, Democratic Republic of Congo, 7 October 2026 -/African Media Agency(AMA)/ -The Strategic Investment Fund of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (“FIS-RDC”), Enterprise Power DRC SARL (“EnPower”), Trafigura and Gridworks Development Partners (together, “the Parties”) have signed a Strategic Framework Agreement to jointly finance, build and operate a 200km high-voltage power line connecting Kalumbila, Zambia, with Kolwezi, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The Kalumbila–Kolwezi Interconnector Project (“KKIP”) will strengthen the DRC’s connection to the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), the regional body that links national grids and allows countries to trade power across borders. The project has reached the final stage of development, with all necessary concessions, licences and authorisations secured. It has an estimated construction cost of USD300 million.
KKIP will deliver benefits on both sides of the border: a new source of reliable, affordable power for the DRC’s mining and industrial sectors, and new export capacity and transmission opportunities for Zambian power producers. The line will have a thermal capacity of 700MW, enabling up to 550MW of competitively priced electricity to be imported into the Copperbelt mining region of the DRC. The line design allows for a future capacity increase to over 1GW.
The Parties and financing
FIS-RDC, EnPower and Gridworks have confirmed their intention to invest equity in KKIP, with Gridworks as lead equity investor and majority shareholder. The Parties are in discussions with Zambian entities about taking a stake in the project. EnPower is the project developer, a licensed Congolese power trader and a SAPP member. Gridworks is a specialist transmission and distribution developer owned and funded by British International Investment, the UK Government’s development finance institution. Trafigura, a market leader in the global commodities industry, has agreed to arrange a significant share of the project’s debt financing.
For FIS-RDC, the transaction supports the DRC Government’s objective of investing in strategic infrastructure with wider economic benefits. It is the first investment announced by FIS-RDC since its creation in October 2025.
Benefits for the DRC
KKIP will help address the country’s structural energy deficit of more than 1GW. It is expected to:
- Supply electricity from across Southern Africa to power Congolese mining and industry, supporting social and economic development in local communities
- Enable the development of mining and refining projects currently on hold due to a lack of available, cost-effective baseload power
- Increase mining and refining output, generating greater fiscal contributions for the DRC
- Deliver broader benefits for the DRC by expanding access to reliable, affordable power for communities and businesses, supporting local enterprise and jobs, and contributing to economic diversification
Benefits for Zambia
KKIP will create export opportunities for Zambian power producers, provide transmission capacity for licensed operators, and help spur the development of new generation. The participation of FIS-RDC, alongside Gridworks and Trafigura, will also strengthen cooperation between the DRC and Zambian governments and create a platform for long-term investment. Discussions are already underway with Zambian entities on potential co-investment.
Emile Osumba, CEO of FIS-RDC, said: “KKIP is the Fund’s inaugural transaction, and it reflects precisely the mandate entrusted to us by the Government. By helping close the Copperbelt’s power deficit, the project will unlock industrial growth, skilled jobs and fiscal revenue for the DRC. By backing a project led by a private Congolese developer, FIS-RDC is demonstrating that sovereign capital can act as a catalyst for private investment rather than a substitute for it. And by co-investing alongside credible and experienced partners such as Gridworks, we are building the track record that will allow the Fund to mobilise further capital for the country’s strategic infrastructure.”
Marc Orphanides, Managing Director of EnPower, added: “This agreement is an important milestone towards executing this strategic transmission infrastructure, which will add significant capacity to meet the ever-growing power demand of the DRC mining industry. We are grateful to the authorities, stakeholders and communities in the DRC and Zambia, as well as the International Finance Corporation, for their support to KKIP, which will be the first privately developed and financed cross-border transmission infrastructure on the African continent.”
Gonzalo De Olazaval, Global Head of Metals and Minerals at Trafigura, commented: “Trafigura is proud to support this landmark power project in the DRC, part of our broader power strategy in Africa. Reliable, competitively priced power is a critical enabler of economic growth across the continent, and Trafigura is well placed to bring together the investment, infrastructure and partnerships needed to make these projects a reality. KKIP has the potential to unlock industrial growth in the DRC and Zambia, while also supporting job creation and local communities in both countries.”
Chris Flavin, CEO of Gridworks, said: “Gridworks is proud to be the lead equity investor in KKIP. This is an important regional integration project. Zambia and the DRC both stand to benefit from closer interconnection, and this project will give the Copperbelt access to reliable, competitively priced power and lay the foundation for further cross-border transmission investment across Southern Africa. While the project is anchored by mining offtake, there is capacity on the line to serve the wider population too. Connecting regional power markets and supporting efficient energy trading is key to sustained economic growth in the region. We look forward to working alongside our partners to deliver this important infrastructure.”

The delegation was received by Egypt’s Deputy Minister of Transport for Railways, the head of the central administration of Sokhna Port and the executive director of the port’s development project. The development program has added around 18 kilometers of berths, cargo-handling yards and logistics zones covering more than 9 million square meters. The corridor passes through major industrial areas and is designed to strengthen multimodal transport connections, enhance the movement of goods and investment, and support Egypt’s role as a regional transit-trade hub.
Egypt-Tanzania Logistics Cooperation

articles.title: Oil, reform and exports: the world's fastest-growing economies in 2026 - qz.com
articles.summary: Oil, reform and exports: the world's fastest-growing economies in 2026  qz.com
articles.full_text:
These 10 economies are projected among the world's fastest-growing in 2026, driven by oil, reform and manufacturing, per World Bank outlooks
The world's fastest-growing economies are almost never its biggest. The World Bank's Global Economic Prospects reports have flagged the same cluster of countries for several years: smaller, resource-rich or export-dependent nations expanding at several times the global average. The Bank has recently put that global average in the range of roughly two to three percent a year. Guyana's offshore oil fields, India's manufacturing and services expansion and Rwanda's long diversification drive are three versions of one story. Growth concentrates where a single sector, a policy shift or a demographic wave is doing outsized work.
Knowing which economies rank among the fastest-growing economies in 2026 per World Bank outlooks matters well beyond bond desks and commodity trading floors. Rapid expansion redraws trade routes and pulls migrant labor toward new construction and factory jobs. It also shapes where multinational firms site their next assembly plant or back-office hub. The same growth marks where extreme poverty is falling quickest — a link the Bank treats as central, since its forecasting feeds its poverty-reduction mandate.
The 10 economies below share four structural drivers that recur across the Bank's regional analysis: hydrocarbon and commodity windfalls, export manufacturing, remittance inflows and deliberate policy reform. Rather than pinning one precise growth figure to each country, each slide explains why that economy keeps appearing near the top of global growth tables. Those numbers move with every quarterly revision. What matters more is what generates the expansion on the ground.
Several carry clear vulnerabilities. Guyana and Senegal depend on crude and gas prices set far from their own capitals. Mozambique's outlook hinges on whether security holds in Cabo Delgado. Bangladesh and Ethiopia have both seen political ruptures interrupt investment decisions. Much of Niger's new export income now moves through a single cross-border pipeline.
Read this as a list of economies to watch in 2026 rather than a fixed ranking. Oil prices, debt servicing costs, insurgency and election cycles can shuffle positions within months. The structural story in each country is steadier, and that is what the slides below set out.
Guyana's oil production keeps it at the top
Illustration: Quartz
Guyana has posted the highest growth rates of any economy on earth for most of the past six years, and the cause is arithmetic as much as geology. A country of fewer than a million people started pumping crude in December 2019, so every production vessel added since lands on a very small national base.
The oil sits in the Stabroek block, roughly 120 miles off the coast. Exxon Mobil operates the consortium developing it, alongside China's CNOOC and Chevron $CVX, which acquired partner Hess in 2025. Output began with the Liza Destiny floating vessel, followed by Liza Unity and the Prosperity unit on the Payara development, with additional phases since. Each vessel produces, stores and offloads crude on its own, so capacity arrives in large steps rather than climbing gradually.
Georgetown has directed early revenue into roads, bridges and a gas-to-energy project at Wales, on the west bank of the Demerara River. That project pipes associated gas onshore to generate power and cut electricity costs, long among the highest in the region. A portion of the proceeds is routed through the Natural Resource Fund, a sovereign savings vehicle. It is meant to hold money back rather than spend it as it arrives — the lesson other producers learned after booms left little behind.
Concentration is the central vulnerability. Crude dominates export earnings and an expanding share of the budget, which ties fiscal planning to a price Guyana does not set. Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, which covers much of Guyana's land mass and sits next to the offshore acreage. That dispute adds a political risk most new producers do not carry.
Construction, services and agriculture have expanded too, evidence that money is circulating beyond the offshore platforms. Whether that broadening holds is the real test. Converting a finite extraction windfall into schools, ports and institutions that outlast the fields is the task facing Guyana for the rest of the decade.
India remains the fastest-growing major economy
Illustration: Quartz
India expands faster than any other economy in the world's top 10, with growth running near seven percent while China, the U.S. and the eurozone sit well below that. No economy of comparable size is moving at that pace.
The expansion rests on three legs rather than one. Services exports are the oldest and deepest. Firms such as Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys have shifted from back-office processing into engineering research, product design and cloud work, which bill at higher rates. Domestic consumption supplies the second leg, drawn from a population above 1.4 billion and a widening urban middle class.
Manufacturing is the newest leg and the one policymakers have pushed hardest. The government's production-linked incentive program pays out against incremental output, and it has drawn smartphone and electronics assembly into the country at scale. Foxconn has expanded iPhone assembly in Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka has become a second base for the same supply chain. India now serves as an alternative assembly location for companies trying to reduce their dependence on Chinese factories.
Digital public infrastructure sits underneath much of this. The Unified Payments Interface handles billions of real-time transactions a month. It has pulled small traders and street vendors onto formal payment rails, cutting the cost of doing business for firms that once ran on cash alone.
The weak points are structural. Job creation lags the number of young people entering the workforce each year, and a large share of the labor force is still tied to low-productivity agriculture. High logistics costs have long narrowed the price advantage of Indian factories against rivals in Vietnam and Thailand. That is one reason the central government has raised capital spending on highways, dedicated freight corridors and ports.
Whether India holds this rate through the decade depends less on demand than on supply. The open questions are whether workers move out of farming, whether land and power bottlenecks clear, and whether electronics investment keeps arriving once incentive payments taper.
Rwanda's diversified economy keeps outperforming
Illustration: Quartz
Rwanda's growth rests on a deliberate shift away from subsistence farming toward services, tourism, minerals and technology. That mix has kept it expanding faster than most of East Africa for more than a decade, with no single commodity setting the pace.
Policy design explains much of it. The government under President Paul Kagame built its strategy around business registration, contract enforcement and investor protections. The World Bank's now-discontinued Doing Business rankings placed Rwanda among the highest-ranked countries on the African continent. Transparency International's corruption perceptions index has also scored Rwanda well against regional peers.
Tourism earns an outsized share of foreign exchange relative to the size of the economy. Gorilla trekking permits in Volcanoes National Park carry a deliberately high price, which caps visitor numbers while raising revenue per visitor. Kigali has built a parallel business in conference tourism. It hosted the 2018 African Union summit where the African Continental Free Trade Area agreement was signed, and the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in 2022. RwandAir and the long-running Bugesera International Airport project are meant to serve that hub ambition.
Tin, tantalum and tungsten compete with coffee and tea as the country's top foreign-currency earners. Processing capacity inside Rwanda has expanded to capture value that once left as unrefined ore.
Technology sits at the center of the longer-term plan. A national fiber-optic backbone reaches across the country's districts, mobile money and fintech licensing have widened, and Kigali Innovation City was designed to pull universities and technology firms onto a single campus.
The constraints are structural. Rwanda is landlocked, so freight moves through Mombasa or Dar es Salaam at considerable cost. It remains a low-income country by World Bank classification, and most of the workforce is still in agriculture. Concessional lending and donor grants fund a meaningful share of public spending. Growth also starts from a low base, which flatters percentage figures.
Rwanda's record is one of steady annual expansion rather than a single boom year.
Ethiopia's reforms are reshaping Africa's second-most populous nation
Illustration: Quartz
Ethiopia's growth now rests on a liberalization program that broke open sectors the state had controlled for decades, starting with telecommunications. The government ended Ethio Telecom's monopoly by licensing Safaricom Ethiopia, a consortium led by the Kenyan mobile operator. That gave the country its first competing network and opened a market of more than 120 million people to foreign capital.
Manufacturing is the second pillar. State-financed industrial parks, most visibly Hawassa Industrial Park in the south, were built to draw garment and textile producers. The pitch was labor costs below those in China or Vietnam. Each park bundles factory space, power connections and customs handling on one site — compensation of a sort for Ethiopia's landlocked geography and its reliance on the port of Djibouti.
Ethiopian Airlines gives the economy an asset few peers have. The carrier ranks among Africa's largest and most consistently profitable. Its hub at Addis Ababa Bole International Airport moves passengers and freight bet

articles.summary: Africa’s mineral powerhouse deploys 8 specialised aircraft as it embarks on a 3-year project to unlock untapped mineral wealth  Business Insider AfricaDRC launches geological survey in push to unlock mineral potential  TimesLIVEDR Congo launches major airborne mineral mapping project  Jacaranda FM
articles.full_text:
- The DRC has launched a three-year programme using eight specialised aircraft to map underground mineral resources.
- The initiative, known as PC2G-RDC, is carried out by Xcalibur Multiphysics Group and was inaugurated under President Félix Tshisekedi.
- Surveys will collect various geophysical data across several regions, initially focusing on Kongo Central, Kwango, Kwilu, Grand Kasaï, and Grand Katanga.
- The project aims to directly identify potential mineral deposits and provide data to guide targeted exploration and reduce risks for mining companies.
The programme, known as the Programme of Aerogeophysical and Geological Mapping of the DRC (PC2G-RDC), is being executed by Spanish-based geophysical company Xcalibur Multiphysics Group SL, which has experience conducting mineral mapping projects across Africa.
Launched on October 5 at Ndolo National Airport in Kinshasa under the patronage of President Félix Tshisekedi, the programme will run for 36 months and collect magnetic, radiometric, gravimetric and electromagnetic data across several parts of the country.
Speaking at the launch, DRC Mines Minister Louis Watum Kabamba said the programme would increase the country’s geoscientific coverage to 46.1%, up from 22.27%, as per Reuters.
According to Xcalibur, the three-year project will cover more than 700,000 square kilometres across Kasai, Kwango, Kongo Central and Katanga, using airborne geophysics, fieldwork and advanced data management to create a new geological baseline for the country and guide investment and long-term development.
Why the DRC is mapping its mineral wealth
The DRC’s national geological mapping project dates back to 2017, when the government signed an initial contract with Xcalibur for airborne geophysical and geological mapping.
The agreement was subsequently amended in 2019 and 2022, with the programme divided into a priority Phase A and an optional Phase B. In January 2026, the government signed a second contract with Xcalibur to advance Phase B, building on the results of the first phase.
The programme is being coordinated by the National Geological Service of Congo under the Ministry of Mines and financed by the Mining Fund for Future Generations (FOMIN).
The aircraft will directly identify potential mineral deposits, while the surveys will generate geological data to pinpoint areas of mineralisation and guide more targeted exploration and drilling.
The government expects the improved geological data to reduce uncertainty and exploration risks for mining companies while giving the state better information for investment and resource-management decisions.
Xcalibur brings an established African track record to the project. The Spanish company has previously carried out airborne magnetic and radiometric surveys in Nigeria and has worked on geophysical projects in several other African countries.
Its role in the DRC comes as Kinshasa seeks greater control and understanding of its geological data. Reuters reported last month that the country was seeking to centralise geological information as part of a broader effort to strengthen state oversight of its mineral resources and attract investment.
The DRC holds major deposits of copper and cobalt and is also believed to have significant reserves of other critical minerals. Yet large parts of its territory remain insufficiently explored.
By combining airborne surveys with geological work on the ground, the government hopes to build a more detailed picture of what lies beneath the country and use that information to guide the next generation of mining investment.

Shettima Woos Investors for Nigeria’s Green Energy Transition
*Nigeria needs $410bn additional investment to achieve net-zero pathway, says Presidency
Michael Olugbode in Abuja
Vice President Kashim Shettima has called for urgent policy reforms, stronger public-private partnerships and innovative risk-sharing mechanisms to attract domestic and foreign investment into Nigeria’s green infrastructure, saying the country requires about $410 billion in additional investment by 2060 to achieve its net-zero pathway.
Shettima made the call on Tuesday at the second edition of the Decarbonising Infrastructure in Nigeria (DIN) Summit in Abuja, where policymakers, development finance institutions, private investors, members of the diplomatic corps and climate experts examined ways of closing the huge financing gap confronting Nigeria’s green transition.
Represented by his Deputy Chief of Staff, Senator Ibrahim Hadejia, the Vice President said the scale of funding required presented not only a challenge but also a significant investment opportunity for domestic and international investors.
“Our Energy Transition Plan estimates that Nigeria will require about $410 billion in additional investment above business-as-usual through 2060 to achieve its net-zero pathway.
“That is a significant financing requirement. But it also tells us something else: there is a very large investment opportunity ahead of us,” Shettima said.
He stressed that while government would remain an important player in financing the transition, it could not provide all the capital required to achieve Nigeria’s long-term energy and infrastructure objectives.
“We need the private sector. We need development finance institutions. We need domestic financial institutions and institutional investors. And, perhaps most importantly, we need projects that are properly prepared and capable of attracting that capital,” he said.
The summit, held at the United Nations House in Abuja, was organised by the Office of the Vice President with support from the National Council on Climate Change and the United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO).
It was themed, “De-risking Green Infrastructure Investment in Nigeria: Enabling Policy, Project Readiness and Risk-Sharing Solutions.”
Shettima said the central issue was no longer simply the availability of ideas, policies or climate ambitions, but the ability to convert them into projects that investors could assess, finance and implement.
He identified the questions investors would ordinarily ask before committing capital, including whether the policy environment was clear, whether the revenue model was credible, whether technical issues had been adequately addressed and how risks would be allocated among the parties involved.
“These are practical questions. And I believe that is where DIN Summit 2.0 can make a useful contribution,” he said.
The Vice President acknowledged that investment in green infrastructure in Nigeria faced policy, financial, technical and institutional challenges, but said the obstacles could be addressed through collaboration among stakeholders.
He said Nigeria’s NDC 3.0 had recognised the need to develop a stronger pipeline of projects with viable financing propositions, increase private-sector participation and improve access to climate finance.
The Presidency also pointed to developments across Africa aimed at using early-stage project preparation, blended finance and risk-sharing mechanisms to attract private capital into green infrastructure.
It cited the African Development Bank’s Alliance for Green Infrastructure in Africa, which is seeking to mobilise $500 million in early-stage blended finance to help develop a project pipeline capable of catalysing substantially larger investments.
The Personal Assistant to the President on Subnational Infrastructure, Mr Musaddiq Adamu, who welcomed participants on behalf of the DIN Summit Steering Committee, said the summit was designed to answer a practical question: what would it take to move green infrastructure projects from ideas to investment?
Adamu said the DIN initiative had evolved considerably since its first edition, with pre-summit workshops conducted across energy, transport, urban development and agriculture.
He recalled that last year’s summit attracted more than 400 stakeholders and resulted in the launch of the first DIN State Summit Report, while engagements generated between project developers and potential investors had already produced tangible outcomes.
One such outcome, he said, followed a presentation by APM Terminals on the electrification of port operations at last year’s summit.
According to him, the engagement subsequently contributed to a $60 million agreement with the Nigerian Ports Authority to advance port electrification, with Onne Port positioned to become Nigeria’s first green port.
“For me, that is an important lesson. The objective is not simply to have a good conversation. The goal is to create real investment opportunity,” Adamu said.
He said Nigeria had “no shortage of ambition”, with policies, plans and ideas already in place, but stressed that the greater challenge was transforming those ideas into projects that investors could understand, finance and deliver.
Adamu said the ultimate value of the summit would be determined by what happened after the event, urging participants to focus on tangible outcomes rather than discussions alone.
The financing challenge was further highlighted by the UNIDO Sub-Regional Representative in Nigeria and ECOWAS, Ambassador Philbert Abaka Johnson, who said Nigeria’s physical infrastructure investment needs were estimated at approximately $3 trillion by 2050.
Johnson, in his opening remarks, said tracked climate finance flows into Nigeria averaged only $2.5 billion annually in 2021 and 2022, compared with estimated annual requirements of $29.7 billion.
This, he said, left an estimated annual financing gap of about $27.2 billion.
He identified policy and regulatory uncertainty, fragmented approval processes, unclear institutional mandates and undefined revenue or offtake arrangements among the factors preventing otherwise credible projects from attracting financing.
“These projects sit at very different stages of maturity, from concepts which require feasibility work to projects ready to seek finance,” Johnson said.
He said the task before stakeholders was to address the constraints sequentially and ensure that projects were developed to a stage where investors could properly assess their risks and financing prospects.
Johnson said UNIDO remained committed to working with the Federal and state governments and other stakeholders beyond the summit to advance identified project pipelines.
He disclosed that the organisation would deploy its Computer Model for Feasibility Analysis and Reporting (COMFAR) software and Digital Investment Promotion Platform to support project development.
According to him, the tools are already being used by more than 11,000 practitioners across 160 countries.
The UNIDO official said the agency’s support for Nigeria’s industrial transformation was anchored on its Programme for Country Partnership (PCP), 2024-2028, signed in Abuja in April 2025 and valued at approximately $175 million.
He said the programme covered industrial policy and strategic governance, start-ups and enterprise development, special economic zones and industrial parks, agricultural and mineral value chains, sustainable energy and environmental management, as well as trade capacity building under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
Johnson said the DIN Summit aligned with the sustainable energy, environmental management, special economic zones and industrial parks components of the programme, stressing that Nigeria’s industrial development and infrastructure decarbonisation agenda were closely connected.
He recalled that the inaugural summit brought together more than 400 stakeholders and produced green investment pipelines and a policy communiqué that strengthened coordination among institutions responsible for Nigeria’s infrastructure and climate priorities.
Johnson specifically called for the operationalisation of the Climate Change Act and sanctity of power purchase agreements as part of efforts to unlock carbon finance in Nigeria and across Africa.
The stakeholders argued that improving project preparation would be critical to attracting private capital, particularly for projects that currently remain at the concept or feasibility stage.
The summit therefore sought to establish a more coordinated approach to identifying, preparing and financing green infrastructure projects, while creating mechanisms for sharing risks between government, development finance institutions and private investors.
The Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change, Mrs Tenioye Majekodunmi, who participated virtually, said green infrastructure had the capacity to create more than 300,000 jobs.
The summit also heard calls for standardised public-private partnership agreement templates and dedicated early-stage project development funding to create a pipeline of bankable projects in mini-grids, clean transportation and green buildings.
Participants stressed that investors needed greater certainty around power purchase agreements, revenue structures, regulatory processes and contractual obligations before committing long-term capital to green infrastructure.
With Nigeria’s green transition requiring hundreds of billions of dollars in additional investment, the summit placed project readiness, policy certainty and risk-sharing at the centre of efforts to mobilise private capital and turn the country’s climate ambitions into investable infrastructure.

articles.title: Africa’s trade ambition runs faster than systems built to support it - Businessamlive
articles.summary: Africa’s trade ambition runs faster than systems built to support it  Businessamlive
articles.full_text:
African leaders are signalling growing confidence in the continent’s commercial future even as the and institutional barriers to doing business across borders remain stubbornly high.
New findings from the 2026 PAFTRAC Africa CEO Trade Survey show that 81.3 percent of senior executives expect their cross-border business activity to increase over the next 12 months, underscoring a strong private-sector appetite for deeper African trade.
Yet the optimism sits against a striking contradiction: intra-African merchandise trade remains broadly stuck at 15–18 percent of total African exports, despite the operational rollout of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
The findings, drawn from more than 2,500 business leaders across the continent, suggest that Africa’s private sector may be ready to trade more with itself, but the infrastructure of finance, payments, policy implementation and market intelligence has yet to catch up with that ambition.
The survey, now in its sixth year, has expanded substantially from 400 respondents in 2021, making its latest edition one of the broadest assessments of African executive sentiment on trade.
Perhaps most significantly, intra-African commerce has emerged as the leading destination priority for surveyed executives, ahead of China, Europe and the United States.
That shift in business orientation could prove important for the continent’s integration agenda. But it also exposes the gap between the market Africa wants to build and the systems businesses currently have to navigate.
The cost of perceived risk
Finance remains one of the most immediate constraints.
According to the survey, 57 percent of executives consider access to trade finance for cross-border transactions difficult or very difficult. For smaller businesses, the challenge is even more consequential, with the International Finance Corporation estimating Africa’s SME financing gap at more than $331 billion.
PAFTRAC argues that the problem is not simply a shortage of capital, but the cost at which African risk is assessed.
Citing International Finance Corporation (IFC) analysis, the organisation estimates that African sovereign and institutional borrowers face an additional $31 billion a year in financing costs because of risk premiums associated with international credit assessments.
Patrick Utomi, a professor of political economy and the chairperson of PAFTRAC, described the issue as a “prejudice premium”, arguing that international risk assessments can fail to adequately reflect conditions on the ground.
“The core issue is risk perception,” Utomi said, arguing that global rules and rating methodologies can impose a direct cost on African economies and, ultimately, on trade.
The implications extend beyond governments.
Higher sovereign borrowing costs can feed through to domestic financial markets, increasing the cost of credit for banks and businesses and making cross-border transactions less competitive. For companies attempting to build regional supply chains, finance an export order or enter a new African market, the cost of capital can therefore become a trade barrier in its own right.
AfCFTA’s implementation test
The survey also points to a second problem: the gap between the existence of continental trade architecture and businesses’ ability to use it.
Some 70.2 percent of respondents said they had experienced a tangible operational impact from AfCFTA-related reforms. But awareness of several of the mechanisms intended to make the agreement work remains limited.
More than half of respondents, according to the preliminary findings, are unfamiliar with the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), which is designed to facilitate cross-border payments in African currencies and reduce reliance on traditional correspondent banking and dollar clearing arrangements.
Awareness is similarly limited around other AfCFTA implementation tools, including the E-Tariff Book, the African Trade Observatory and mechanisms for reporting non-tariff barriers.
That creates an important distinction between policy implementation and commercial adoption.
A trade agreement can remove tariffs on paper, but businesses still need to know where opportunities exist, understand the applicable rules, obtain financing, make payments efficiently and resolve regulatory or logistical obstacles.
Without those supporting systems, tariff liberalisation alone is unlikely to deliver the scale of intra-African commerce envisaged by policymakers.
Confidence meets capacity
The survey therefore presents a picture of an African private sector that is neither disengaged nor pessimistic about regional trade.
Quite the opposite. Executives appear increasingly willing to look beyond traditional external markets and build commercial relationships within Africa. The constraint is that the institutions supporting those ambitions remain unevenly understood and, in some cases, expensive to access.
That distinction matters. The next phase of AfCFTA implementation will be judged not only by the agreements governments sign or the policies they adopt, but by whether can actually use the resulting systems at competitive cost.
For African companies, the test is ultimately practical: can an exporter in one African country find a buyer in another, secure affordable trade finance, navigate customs and regulatory requirements, receive payment efficiently and scale the relationship without prohibitive friction?
The PAFTRAC findings suggest there is already significant demand for that market.
What remains uncertain is whether Africa’s and policy architecture can move quickly enough to meet it.
The full 2026 PAFTRAC Africa CEO Trade Survey, expected later this month, is set to provide a broader assessment of the continent’s trade barriers, progress on AfCFTA implementation and financing constraints, alongside private-sector policy recommendations based on responses from more than 2,500 executives.

President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi meets South Korean President Lee Jae Myung in Seoul, 8 Oct. 2026. Presidency
CAIRO – 8 October 2026: Egypt and South Korea on Thursday announced the elevation of their relations to a strategic partnership and launched negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).
The two countries made the announcement as President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and his South Korean counterpart, Lee Jae Myung, held summit talks during El-Sisi's official visit to Seoul.
Speaking at a joint press conference after the talks, El-Sisi said the upgrade opens the way for a promising future to the firm Egyptian-Korean ties based on mutual respect and shared interests.
He said the move reflects the importance both countries attach to advancing their relations and will open new prospects for Egyptian-Korean cooperation across political, economic and development fields.
El-Sisi said the partnership comes within the framework of Egypt’s balanced and diversified foreign policy, which is based on strategic balance and seeks to develop relations with all countries on the principles of mutual respect and shared benefit.
Meanwhile, the partnership would contribute to supporting international peace and security and preserving the foundations of the international order based on the principles and provisions of international law, El-Sisi stressed.
He added that the partnership would contribute to promoting development and prosperity for the peoples of Egypt and South Korea, as well as the world.
“Today in Seoul, we issued a joint statement elevating our bilateral relations to a strategic partnership,” Lee said during the press conference.
Lee added that they also “agreed to turn our previous agreements into tangible outcomes for the people of both countries,” according to Korea’s Yonhap News Agency.
Areas of cooperation
Under the strategic partnership, Egypt and South Korea agreed to deepen and expand future cooperation across several areas, including political, defense, economic, developmental, cultural, educational, regional and international cooperation, according to the joint statement.
First: Political cooperation
The two countries will strengthen high-level political exchanges and communication at various levels. These include continued dialogue and consultations between their foreign ministries on strategic cooperation and issues of shared interest at the bilateral, regional and international levels.
The two sides welcomed the first strategic dialogue between their foreign ministers, held in Seoul on June 2 and agreed to continue discussions and follow up on progress across various aspects of bilateral relations.
Second: Defense cooperation
Egypt and South Korea welcomed continued cooperation in the defense sector and agreed to pursue further progress in defense industries.
Third: Economic and development cooperation
The two countries reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening trade and investment ties as a key pillar of comprehensive economic cooperation.
The two leaders welcomed the launch of negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).
Egypt and South Korea will also work to expand cooperation across manufacturing — particularly shipbuilding and electric vehicles — as well as energy, infrastructure, advanced technology, AI, smart cities, development of the Suez Canal Economic Zone and industrial localization, while increasing investment in these areas.
The two sides recognized Egypt’s strategic importance as a gateway to Africa and highlighted the potential to expand trilateral cooperation between Egypt, South Korea and African countries.
Fourth: Cultural and educational cooperation
The two countries will continue implementing cooperation under existing memoranda of understanding in culture and education.
They affirmed their commitment to encouraging greater cultural exchanges based on their rich cultural assets, including creative content and historical heritage.
They also agreed to designate 2027 as a year of cultural exchanges.
Egypt and South Korea expressed their commitment to developing educational programs, including scholarships, Korean-language education and youth training initiatives.
The two sides will work to strengthen technical and vocational education and training programs in Egypt in line with labor market needs and sustainable development.
Fifth: Regional and international cooperation
Egypt and South Korea reaffirmed their commitment to working together to promote peace and stability in the Middle East and on the Korean Peninsula.
They also agreed to continue strategic dialogue on regional and international issues of shared interest, including the Palestinian issue, water security, developments in the Horn of Africa, Yemen and Libya, and freedom of international navigation, in accordance with international law.
The two countries said the strategic partnership marks a new phase in bilateral relations, opening broad prospects for fruitful cooperation that benefits the peoples of Egypt and South Korea and contributes to stability and prosperity.

articles.title: China’s BRI Cuts Both Ways for Authoritarian Rule - The China-Global South Project
articles.summary: China’s BRI Cuts Both Ways for Authoritarian Rule  The China-Global South Project
articles.full_text:
- Chinese BRI investment can reinforce entrenched authoritarian rule by bolstering patronage networks and developmental legitimacy, exemplified by Cambodia's CPP.
- Chinese investment can fuel corruption scandals, elite fractures and opposition mobilization, as with Najib's projects and Barisan Nasional's defeat in Malaysia.
- Regime outcomes are contingent; BRI's political effects depend on existing political settlements, elite cohesion and contestation strength.
By Neil Loughlin
China’s rise has intensified debate over whether its growing economic influence promotes authoritarianism internationally. Critics have portrayed President Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) as supporting authoritarian partners, weakening democratic pressure and helping construct a more autocratic international order. But while Chinese investment has reinforced authoritarian governments in some cases, it has intensified political conflict and weakened incumbent regimes in others.
Economic and political ties to powerful authoritarian states can provide governments with material support during instability, reinforce patronage networks and reduce the impact of international pressure. Yet the potential for external material investment to destabilize authoritarian regimes has received less attention.
Unequal resource allocation can generate intra-elite tensions, while those excluded from patronage networks or economic opportunities may align with opposition movements. In analyzing how external investment becomes part of existing struggles over power and resources, a key consideration is identifying who benefits from investment and how this aligns with the prevailing political and economic system.
Cambodia and Malaysia illustrate these dynamics because both received Chinese investment after 2013 while their long-ruling electoral authoritarian governments faced serious political crises. Both regimes relied on patronage, clientelism and performance-based legitimacy to sustain ruling coalitions. Chinese investment might have been expected to reinforce incumbent authoritarian rule in both cases. Instead, their political trajectories diverged.
In Cambodia, the closely contested July 2013 election posed the strongest challenge to the Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) in decades. The opposition Cambodia National Rescue Party won almost 45 percent of the vote, while workers, farmers, youth and other groups joined a broader protest movement against CPP rule. The government responded by suppressing dissent, restricting civil society and dissolving the main opposition party through the Supreme Court in 2017, leaving the CPP virtually unopposed in the 2018 election.
Chinese investment expanded during this crisis and entered a political economy dominated by a closely connected state–party apparatus, business tycoons and the security forces. Politically connected Cambodian firms became local partners in Chinese-backed infrastructure, industrial and property projects. These arrangements reinforced existing patronage networks and gave leading economic elites a material interest in the continuation of CPP rule.
Chinese-funded projects also supported the CPP’s claims to developmental legitimacy. Then-prime minister Hun Sen presented infrastructure and economic growth as evidence that political stability produced national progress. Labor mobilization, environmental protests and opposition politics could be portrayed as threats to development. Chinese finance expanded as US and EU critics highlighted the Cambodian government’s repression and threatened sanctions or trade restrictions. Chinese investment helped maintain elite cohesion and reduced the costs of Western pressure.
Malaysia followed a different path. Before 2018, the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition had dominated the country under a system of repressive but competitive electoral authoritarianism. Elections heavily favored the ruling coalition, but opposition parties could compete and mobilize. The political settlement between the BN and its principal party, the United Malays National Organization, was already fragmenting. Its dominance had weakened after the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, the rise of the Reformasi movement and chronic divisions within the ruling elite. Civil society organizations had also developed the capacity to mobilize public dissatisfaction.
Then-prime minister Najib Razak initially appeared to be offered a lifeline by the post-2014 increase in Chinese investment into Malaysia. Large infrastructure projects could generate contracts for government-linked companies, reward political allies and reinforce the coalition’s developmental credentials. But Chinese investment also became embroiled in the political and financial crises that helped end BN’s dominance.
The long-envisioned East Coast Rail Link connecting Kuala Lumpur with cities in the east of Peninsular Malaysia was revived by Najib’s government in 2016 with Chinese financing. The scheme’s budget was alleged to have been inflated partly to help cover debts generated through the misuse of funds from the 1Malaysia Development Berhad state investment vehicle. Other China-linked investment projects, including Johor’s Forest City development, also raised concerns surrounding foreign ownership, sovereignty and the distribution of benefits.
These controversies saw Chinese investment feed into domestic political conflicts that long predated the BRI. Najib sought to use Chinese capital to preserve patronage networks and stabilize his ruling coalition, while his opponents — including Mahathir Mohamad and the Pakatan Harapan opposition bloc — presented the same investments as evidence of corruption, economic mismanagement and threats to national sovereignty.
The opposition’s organization ensured elections remained sufficiently competitive. These grievances contributed to BN’s defeat in May 2018.
Malaysia’s post-2018 governments nevertheless continued to seek access to Chinese investment. Mahathir renegotiated several major BRI projects, while subsequent governments also remained supportive of Malaysia’s involvement in the BRI. The more competitive political environment only altered the struggles over how BRI investment was distributed and controlled.
The contrast in political outcomes linked to BRI investment in Cambodia and Malaysia highlights the need for caution when drawing simplistic conclusions about the authoritarian effects of Chinese investment. BRI investment may reinforce the political status quo where elites maintain stable coalitions and effectively subdue dissent, as seen in Cambodia. Where elite power is fractured, weak, or contested, as it was in Malaysia, outside investment can instead undermine an authoritarian regime if the forces contesting it are strong enough.
Authoritarian outcomes linked to Chinese investment are not inevitable, but largely depend on how such investments interact with existing political settlements and political economy dynamics in recipient states. External investment alone did not determine regime outcomes — instead, it became part of ongoing internal political conflicts, amplifying underlying mechanisms of political control and contestation.
Neil Loughlin is Senior Lecturer in Comparative Politics at City St George’s, University of London. articles.title: Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata (SMP Kolkata), in association with the Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI), organised a road show on 7 October 2026 to present the proposed development of the Extended Port Gate System at Balagarh, West Ben - Maritime Gateway
articles.summary: Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata (SMP Kolkata), in association with the Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI), organised a road show on 7 October 2026 to present the proposed development of the Extended Port Gate System at Balagarh, West Ben  Maritime Gateway
articles.full_text:
Held at The Bengal Club in Kolkata, the event brought together government representatives, port stakeholders, trade partners and logistics companies to discuss the proposed port infrastructure project. Shri Subrata Gupta, Advisor to the Hon’ble Chief Minister of West Bengal, attended the event as Chief Guest, while Shri Rathendra Raman, Chairman, SMP Kolkata, welcomed him. Representatives from Adani, JSW Infrastructure, IWAI and other logistics companies participated in the programme. The Deputy Chairman and senior officers of SMP Kolkata were also present.
Addressing the gathering, Shri Subrata Gupta, Advisor to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, West Bengal, said, “Balagarh is a unique example of Centre-State coordination.” He added that rail, road and waterways connectivity is being provided by the Central Government, while industrial land is being made available by the State Government. He also said that environmental clearance has already been obtained and that coordination between the Central and State Governments would help the project support trade, industry and West Bengal.
Shri Rathendra Raman, Chairman, SMP Kolkata, said that Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi had recently laid the foundation stone for the Inland Water Transport (IWT) Terminal and Road Over Bridge at Balagarh. He said, “The project will decongest Kolkata Dock System (KDS) and being waterways-based, it will be environment friendly and sustainable.”
The Balagarh project has an estimated cost of Rs. 538.20 crore and a planned cargo-handling capacity of 2.7 million tonnes per annum (MTPA). Located around 85 km upstream of the Kolkata Dock System on National Waterway-1, the project is intended to strengthen inland waterway connectivity and provide an extended gateway for cargo movement.
The road show received participation from trade partners as SMP Kolkata and IWAI presented the project’s infrastructure and connectivity proposition to potential stakeholders.
What is the Balagarh Extended Port Gate System?
The Balagarh Extended Port Gate System is a proposed port infrastructure project in West Bengal designed to extend cargo-handling and port connectivity capabilities upstream of the Kolkata Dock System. The project will use National Waterway-1 and associated road and rail connectivity to facilitate cargo movement.
Key Details of the Balagarh Project
- Location: Balagarh, West Bengal
- Project cost: Rs. 538.20 crore
- Planned capacity: 2.7 MTPA
- Distance from KDS: Approximately 85 km upstream
- Waterway: National Waterway-1
- Key stakeholders: SMP Kolkata and IWAI
- Infrastructure: IWT Terminal and Road Over Bridge
- Environmental clearance: Obtained

articles.full_text:
Gemcorp and the Fonds Souverain Malagasy (“FSM”) signed a strategic partnership during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (“UNGA”) in New York, establishing a framework to support investment and the development of Madagascar’s strategic assets.
Under the leadership of His Excellency Michael Randrianirina, President of the Republic of Madagascar and guided by his vision to “transform the potential and endowments of the country into tangible impacts for the people,” the partnership will support FSM and the Government of Madagascar in advancing the country’s growth and investment agenda. This includes a particular focus on unlocking the value of Madagascar’s mineral resources, alongside its broader assets across mining, energy and infrastructure.
As part of this partnership, FSM and the Government of Madagascar will set the strategic direction and priorities, with Gemcorp supporting FSM in structuring projects, developing investment and financing solutions, and connecting projects with international sources of capital, investors and partners.
The partnership is intended to help attract foreign direct investment and long-term international capital into projects, supporting Madagascar’s economic development and the sustainable realisation of its natural resources.
His Excellency Andry Raharinomena, Chairman of FSM, said:
“Madagascar is actively building strategic partnerships and attracting investment. We have assets across energy, infrastructure and mining, and FSM is determined to work with world-class partners to realise their full potential. This agreement with Gemcorp marks an important step forward, and we look forward to building on this partnership together.”
Atanas Bostandjiev, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Gemcorp, said:
“We are delighted to enter into this partnership with FSM. Madagascar has the ambition, the leadership and the strategic assets to become one of Africa’s leading investment destinations, and we look forward to helping FSM bring the world’s capital to its priority projects. This is the kind of partnership Gemcorp is built for: we bring financing and structuring, commodities trading and offtake, industrial operations and advisory, backed by a real presence on the ground, to help turn national priorities into investable projects and, ultimately, delivered outcomes for the Malagasy people.”
Madagascar has meaningful potential across critical minerals, energy and infrastructure. Working alongside FSM, the partnership will focus on translating selected objectives into well-structured bankable projects – with the commercial, financing and delivery foundations that give international partners the confidence to invest for the long term.
About Gemcorp
Gemcorp is an integrated investment and operating group focused on emerging markets. Founded in 2014, we originate, structure, finance, invest in and operate strategic businesses and infrastructure across the emerging markets - combining proprietary capital with capital managed for institutional and private investors.
Across five complementary divisions - asset management, commodities trading, principal investments, operational assets, and critical supply and logistics - Gemcorp pairs deep local presence with the capital and operating capability to deliver in markets where others will not. With teams across Africa, the Middle East and Latin America, we turn undercapitalized opportunities into lasting value for our investors and durable growth in the economies where we operate.

articles.full_text:

09 Oct 2026, 07:01 GMT+10
            
Addis Ababa [Ethiopia], October 9 (ANI): External Affairs Minister (EAM) S Jaishankar on Thursday (local time) arrived in Ethiopia as part of his three-nation tour of African countries, expressing hope for productive engagements to advance India's strategic partnership with the East African nation.
"Hello Addis Ababa! Delighted to arrive in Ethiopia. Thank State Minister @BerhanuTsegaye for the warm reception. Look forward to productive engagements to advance our Strategic Partnership," Jaishankar said in a post on X.
Ethiopia is the third and final leg of Jaishankar's three-nation African tour, which also included visits to Ghana and Cote d'Ivoire.
During his visit to Cote d'Ivoire, Jaishankar highlighted India's developmental engagement with African countries, emphasising that New Delhi's approach has been guided by the needs and priorities of its African partners.
Addressing alumni of the Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) programme in Cote d'Ivoire, Jaishankar said India's development partnership with Africa has remained central to its engagement with the continent.
"Where Africa is concerned, development partnership has always been central to our engagement, and we have taken a view that what we do in India should respond to the demands and priorities of our African partners," he said.
He also referred to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's articulation of the Kampala principles of India's engagement with Africa.
Jaishankar said ITEC serves as a platform for sharing India's developmental, security and governance experiences, along with best practices, technology and expertise.
"ITEC is very important because it is a vehicle to share our developmental experiences, our security experiences, our governance experiences, best practices, to also discuss technology and expertise together," he said.
He added that the programme also enabled India to learn from participants from partner countries, noting that their presence benefited the institutions where they received training.
The External Affairs Minister said ITEC, which began in 1964, marked its 62nd anniversary this year. The programme covers more than 160 partner nations and provides nearly 10,000 fully funded training opportunities annually across various fields.
Jaishankar said the programme covered areas ranging from information and communication technology, digital governance and public administration to agriculture, energy, skill development, defence, security and counterterrorism.
During his engagements in Cote d'Ivoire, Jaishankar also met Vice Prime Minister and Defence Minister Tene Birahima Ouattara to discuss the growing defence partnership between the two countries.
He held discussions with Cote d'Ivoire's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Niale Kaba in Abidjan, focusing on strengthening bilateral cooperation in trade, investment, infrastructure, agriculture, healthcare and people-to-people ties.
Jaishankar said Cote d'Ivoire was one of India's key partners in West Africa and reiterated New Delhi's support for the country's economic growth, governance transformation, and security and defence objectives.
He highlighted the role of capacity-building initiatives in strengthening long-term ties between the two countries, noting that around 800 ITEC training slots had been utilised by Cote d'Ivoire over the preceding 12 years.
The minister said human connections and shared experiences built through such programmes were important to sustaining bilateral relations. (ANI)

articles.title: Nestlé Ghana expands Tema factory, raises evaporated milk production capacity - MyJoyOnline
articles.summary: Nestlé Ghana expands Tema factory, raises evaporated milk production capacity  MyJoyOnline
articles.full_text:
Audio By Carbonatix
Nestlé Ghana has expanded its Tema factory with a new evaporated milk production line, significantly increasing the company’s capacity to manufacture one of its major products locally.
The new line, commissioned by President John Dramani Mahama on Thursday, October 8, 2026, replaces a production line that had been in operation for more than 30 years.
The expansion will increase the factory’s annual evaporated milk production capacity from approximately 12,960 tonnes to nearly 30,000 tonnes.
The upgraded facility will undertake the filling, homogenisation, sterilisation and packaging of milk locally, with the processes carried out by Ghanaian workers.
President Mahama, who commissioned the facility, described the investment as an important demonstration of Ghana’s capacity to produce more of what it consumes and strengthen local manufacturing.
He said the expansion was also consistent with the government’s 24-hour economy initiative, which seeks to promote continuous production, increase industrial activity and create jobs.
The President urged Nestlé to leverage Ghana’s position as the headquarters of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to expand its reach into markets across the continent.
He said the expanded production line gives the company the capacity to increase its contribution to Ghana’s ambition of becoming a production hub for Africa.
President Mahama also stressed the importance of protecting local manufacturers from illicit imports and customs evasion, particularly as domestic production capacity increases.
The Nestlé Tema factory has been in operation since 1970 and produces a range of products for the Ghanaian market and export markets across Central and West Africa.
The expansion comes amid renewed industrial activity in Tema, which President Mahama says is gradually regaining its position as Ghana’s major industrial centre.
He cited developments including the expansion of the Tema Port, efforts to revive the Tema Oil Refinery and ongoing work to restore the Volta Aluminium Company (VALCO) as part of the industrial activity taking place in the enclave.
The Minister for Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, Elizabeth Ofosu-Adjare, also highlighted growing investment activity in Ghana, saying foreign direct investment inflows increased from US$652 million in 2024 to US$2.62 billion in 2025.
She said the manufacturing sector recorded the highest number of new investment projects in 2025, with 99 projects, ahead of mining, oil and gas, and general trade.
Speaking at the commissioning ceremony, the Managing Director of Nestlé Ghana Limited, Salomé Azevedo, said the investment reflected the company’s confidence in Ghana and its long-term commitment to local manufacturing.
“Today is a proud moment for all of us—a milestone that reflects our deep confidence in Ghana, our enduring commitment to local manufacturing and our belief in the bright future of this country,” she said.
She said the expansion demonstrated that products made in Ghana could meet international standards and compete effectively in regional and global markets.
According to Ms Azevedo, the investment was ultimately about the people who depend on the company’s products, noting the important place evaporated milk occupies in the daily lives of Ghanaian families.
She said the project also represented the efforts of the employees who planned, installed and tested the new production line, as well as those responsible for operating it while maintaining safety and quality standards.
Ms Azevedo said Nestlé’s presence in Ghana dates back to 1957, the year the country gained independence, while the Tema factory was commissioned in 1971, with IDEAL Milk among the first products manufactured there.
She said the latest investment builds on that history and strengthens local value creation while creating opportunities across the company’s value chain.
“This investment builds on a legacy of shared progress, strengthens local value creation, creates opportunities across our value chain and reinforces Ghana’s position as a competitive manufacturing destination,” she said.
The Managing Director also highlighted Nestlé Ghana’s environmental initiatives, saying the Tema factory had achieved zero waste to landfill and operates on 100 per cent green energy.
She added that the company was working with partners to collect and recycle more plastic than it puts on the market, as part of efforts to reduce its environmental footprint.
The expansion of Nestlé’s Tema factory therefore adds to the growing push for increased domestic manufacturing, value addition and export-oriented production in Ghana.
