articles.title: France and Germany float 'trade bazooka' against China as the EU scrambles to confront its exports - Fortune
articles.summary: France and Germany float 'trade bazooka' against China as the EU scrambles to confront its exports  Fortune
articles.full_text:
The European Union is bracing for a confrontation with China as a trade deficit exceeding $1 billion a day heightens anxiety over potential job losses and pushes the bloc’s political leaders to take a more aggressive approach toward its second-largest trading partner.
The European Commission’s top trade envoy, Maroš Šefčovič, will be in Beijing Thursday for a two-day meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. The goal is narrowing the EU’s 360 billion euro ($410 billion) trade deficit with China. Earlier this year, he gave Beijing a deadline of October to provide meaningful results in doing so.
Politicians and economists across the 27-nation bloc consider China’s massive subsidies and exports a major threat to core industrial sectors from steel foundries to car factories. China diverted many of its exports to the EU and other markets after the U.S. raised tariffs.
In a debate Tuesday in European Parliament in Strasbourg, lawmakers overwhelmingly expressed anxiety alongside defiance over trade with China. On Wednesday, they voted 454 to 86 on a resolution to toughen up on China that centered on a call for “economic reciprocity and a proportionate EU response if China does not open its markets.”
Ahead of the vote, Hilde Vautmans, the Belgian lawmaker who led the resolution, said that “Europe has economic power, it’s time we used it.”
EU options range from tariffs to a “trade bazooka”
Despite the seeming European unity this week, it remains unclear what the EU can or is willing to do. It has already rolled out trade measures against Chinese steel imports and e-commerce small parcels.
France’s High Commission for Strategy and Planning in February called for swift action, like 30% tariffs on many of China’s exports, and a devaluation of the euro against the Chinese currency. Sales of German autos are plummeting in China, but China is also poised to gobble up market share in Europe by undercutting European automakers on price thanks to heavy state subsidies. There have already been mass layoffs at major manufacturers like Volkswagen.
A letter by France and Germany, a copy of which was seen by The Associated Press, called for a sweeping rethink of the EU’s China policy. Among other actions, it proposed making it easier for the European Commission to use the bloc’s so-called “trade bazooka,” the Anti-Coercion Instrument. This is a never-used-before raft of measures for blocking or restricting trade and investment from countries found to be putting undue pressure on EU member nations or corporations.
Yet not all EU nations agree on such tough measures. Spain, the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy, has been less adversarial toward China in recent years. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited Beijing four times in three years. Far-right and left-wing lawmakers from Ireland to Bulgaria formed an unusual coalition on Wednesday to vote against resolution calling for tougher China policies.
The European Policy Centre in Brussels said in June that European battery producers, solar panels, steel, electric vehicles, chemicals and machinery are already hemorrhaging jobs and capacity and called for a trade investigative body modelled on Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the phenomenon another “ China shock ” for Europe, similar to what happened in the U.S. in the early 2000s when hundreds of thousands of factory jobs in the American heartland were wiped out.
The EU’s ailing economy requires both a domestic overhaul and a more aggressive foreign trade policy, especially with China, said Tim Rühlig, a China analyst at the European Union Institute for Security Studies, the bloc’s internal think tank.
Rühlig also said that European businesses and political leadership bear some blame.
“It’s clear that just protecting yourself from China is not the future,” Rühlig said. “But to have a chance of making yourself ready for future technologies and to remain competitive in the coming 15-20 years, you have to protect yourself.”
It is impossible to disengage completely with China as the EU did with Russia following its invasion of Ukraine, Rühlig said, but there is robust momentum now to reset trade relations with Beijing.
“Where do we make ourselves independent or at least more diverse? And where do we still work with the Chinese?” Rühlig asked.
On Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio during his Greece visit called for Europe to strengthen its alliance with the U.S. as he urged Europe to “awaken from its long slumber.”
Rubio said that Europe and the U.S. are at “a crossroads” where actions taken now “will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.”
China is ready for a long trade dispute
This week in Beijing, when asked about the letter penned by France and Germany, a spokesperson at China’s Ministry of Commerce said that the countries should refrain from encouraging the EU to resort to protectionist measures.
“Protectionism cannot enhance competitiveness, and decoupling or cutting off supply chains will only harm others without benefiting oneself,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.
China is the EU’s second-largest goods trading partner after the U.S., according to European Commission data. Chinese exports to the EU rose 15.3% in the first eight months of this year, according to China’s customs agency, while its imports from the EU rose 6.2%.
“The EU does not have the capacity to wage a trade war against China,” read an editorial last month in China’s state-run Global Times newspaper. “If it is truly determined to do so, then let it try.”
China’s exports to Europe, as well as Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa, expanded after U.S. tariffs went into effect last year, but it still booked a $1.2 trillion trade surplus globally in 2025. So far, China’s export machine has remained remarkably resilient despite U.S. tariffs and other trade restrictions, said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board.
This past weekend, ahead of the meeting between Šefčovič and Wang, China launched an anti-dumping probe on EU exports of p-nitrotoluene, which is used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. The probe was initiated after Beijing warned last month that it would take retaliatory actions if the EU instituted tougher protectionist trade measures.
“China has been battle-tested by successive rounds of external pressure and, so far, has largely stared down attempts to force a change in course,” said Zenglein.
China’s economy has been largely driven by exports as domestic demand remains sluggish. The EU imports sizable amounts of Chinese lithium-ion batteries and hybrid electric vehicles, and Chinese carmakers are also expanding production capacity in Europe.
While China’s trade surplus has intensified concerns among its major trading partners, trade ties between the U.S. and China appear relatively stable following a summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump in Washington, wrote Bank of America economists, turning the attention to China-EU relations.
When it comes to negotiations with the EU, Chinese investment in Europe is likely to be among Beijing’s bargaining chips, Zenglein added, particularly as EU member states compete to attract capital, jobs, and new manufacturing projects.
___
Chan reported from Hong Kong.

articles.title: Russia-Africa Summit: The Search for Resources, Influence and War Resilience - Modern Ghana
articles.summary: Russia-Africa Summit: The Search for Resources, Influence and War Resilience  Modern Ghana
articles.full_text:
Russia's renewed engagement with Africa should be understood against the backdrop of a war in Ukraine that has become a test of Moscow's economic, military and political endurance. Since the invasion of Ukraine, Russia has faced extensive Western sanctions, restrictions on trade and finance, and increasing pressure on the sources of revenue that sustain its war effort. In this environment, Africa has acquired a significance that extends beyond traditional diplomacy. The continent offers Moscow political partnerships, alternative markets, military cooperation and, critically, access to valuable natural resources and potential revenue streams that can help Russia withstand external pressure.
This helps explain the evolution of the Russia-Africa summits. The first summit, held in Sochi in 2019, was largely presented as an effort to rebuild and institutionalise Russia's relationship with Africa, with trade, investment, security and political cooperation at the centre of the agenda. By the time of the second summit in St Petersburg in 2023, however, the geopolitical context had changed dramatically. Russia was already deep into its war in Ukraine and under extensive Western sanctions. The summit therefore served not only to deepen economic and political relations but also to demonstrate that Moscow remained capable of maintaining significant partnerships outside the Western bloc.
The third summit schedule on 28-29 October 2026, comes at an even more consequential moment. Russia is seeking to demonstrate that its relationship with Africa has survived the prolonged Ukraine war and remains capable of producing strategic benefits. The question for African governments should increasingly be whether the relationship is producing comparable benefits for them. Moscow's partnership with Africa cannot be assessed only through diplomatic declarations, military agreements or high-level summits. It should also be judged by what African states receive in return and by what Russia gains from the relationship.
One of the most important areas to examine is natural resources. Russia's interest in Africa is not simply about obtaining diplomatic support. Access to gold and other strategic commodities can provide alternative sources of revenue at a time when Moscow is seeking to reduce the impact of Western sanctions. Gold is particularly important because it can be traded through opaque networks and converted into revenue outside conventional financial channels. The U.S. Treasury has previously linked Wagner-associated gold operations in Africa to the financing of the group's activities, including its operations in Ukraine. This does not mean that every Russian engagement with an African resource-producing state is designed to finance the Ukraine war. It does, however, demonstrate why African resources can have strategic value for a Russia seeking to sustain its power and resilience under sanctions. The same logic extends beyond gold. Russia has increasingly shown interest in energy and critical raw materials, while its security partnerships in countries such as Mali and the Central African Republic have created relationships in which military and political cooperation can intersect with economic and resource interests. The emerging model therefore deserves closer scrutiny, Russia provides security assistance and political backing, while gaining influence, commercial opportunities and potentially privileged access to resources.
Mali provides one of the clearest case studies. Russia's military presence in the country began with the arrival of Wagner personnel in 2021 and subsequently evolved into the Africa Corps structure. Moscow has presented this relationship as an alternative to Western security partnerships and as evidence of Russia's willingness to assist African states in defending their sovereignty. Yet the relationship also raises a fundamental question: what does Russia receive in return for its military and political support?
That question becomes particularly important when the wider context of the Ukraine war is considered. If Russia can secure access to gold and other strategic resources, strengthen relationships with resource-rich governments and establish alternative economic channels, those relationships can help Moscow mitigate the effects of sanctions and sustain its broader strategic capacity. The relationship should therefore not be viewed solely through the narrow lens of counterterrorism. It is also part of a wider contest over resources, influence and economic resilience.
The economic figures contained in the summit case study reinforce the need to ask what kind of partnership Moscow is actually building. At the 2019 Sochi summit, Vladimir Putin announced a target of increasing Russia-Africa trade to $40 billion. According to Russian data cited in the document, trade stood at $27.7 billion in 2025, while Russia accounted for less than 1 percent of foreign direct investment in Africa. These figures do not prove that Russia's Africa strategy has failed, nor do they capture every form of strategic value that Moscow derives from the continent. If Russia's conventional economic footprint remains relatively modest, why is Moscow investing so heavily in strategic relationships with African states? One answer is that the value of Africa to Russia cannot be measured by trade and investment alone. Political influence, military access, diplomatic support, alternative markets and access to natural resources can all have strategic value. For a country fighting a prolonged war under sanctions, these forms of influence can become as important as conventional economic indicators.
This is why the third Russia-Africa Summit should be examined as more than another diplomatic gathering. Moscow wants to use the summit to demonstrate that its partnership with Africa remains strong despite the Ukraine war. The circumstances surrounding the meeting expose the tension at the heart of that claim. African officials are being asked to travel to Moscow while Ukrainian drone attacks have repeatedly disrupted air traffic around the Russian capital. On September 20 an attack involving more than 450 drones caused fresh disruption in the Moscow region, while Air Tanzania temporarily suspended its Moscow route following a risk assessment. The irony is difficult to ignore. Russia presents itself as a security partner for Africa, yet some African officials must consider their own security when travelling to the Russian capital. More importantly, African governments must now assess whether the strategic benefits of their relationship with Moscow justify the risks and costs associated with it.
For Ghana, this calculation is particularly important. The security consequences of Russia's growing involvement in the Sahel cannot be separated from Ghana's own national and regional security interests. A source close to the Ghanaian delegation cited in the summit document questions whether the relationship is genuinely "win-win" and points directly to the deteriorating security situation in the Sahel and its spillover towards Ghana's northern borders. This should concern African governments is Russia's engagement with Africa primarily delivering security and development benefits to African states, or is Africa increasingly becoming an important source of the political influence, strategic resources and economic resilience that Moscow needs to sustain its own geopolitical ambitions?
The answer is unlikely to be simple. Russia's relationship with Africa serves multiple purposes, and resource access is only one component of a broader strategy. But the Ukraine war has changed the calculation. What may once have been presented principally as an effort to expand trade, investment and diplomatic relations now also has to be viewed through the lens of Russia's need to preserve strategic autonomy, withstand sanctions and maintain the capacity to wage a prolonged war.
The third Russia-Africa Summit therefore represents a test not simply of whether African leaders will continue to engage Moscow, but of whether Russia can convince them that this engagement is genuinely reciprocal. For African states, the critical question is no longer whether Russia wants a deeper relationship with Africa. It clearly does. The more important question is what Moscow needs from Africa, what Africa receives in return, and whether the balance between the two is becoming increasingly unequal.
Joseph McCarthy is an analyst and researcher specialising in governance, security and political transitions in the Sahel. He writes on geopolitics, development and African diplomacy. joecarthy30@gmail.com

articles.title: M-KOPA Buys KilpiTek: What It Means for Ghana Phones - JBKlutse
articles.summary: M-KOPA Buys KilpiTek: What It Means for Ghana Phones  JBKlutse
articles.full_text:
Ghanaian phone buyers who pay small amounts daily for a smartphone should take note: Kenyan pay-as-you-go company M-KOPA has bought Finnish software firm KilpiTek Oy for USD 8 million, taking full control of the technology that locks financed phones when repayments stop.
M-KOPA acquired 100% of KilpiTek’s voting shares on March 26 in a cash-and-stock deal, according to its financial disclosures. The company paid USD 2.67 million in cash, with the rest in equity, deferred payments and staff remuneration.
The Finnish company builds device-locking software. In simple terms, it lets a lender remotely restrict or switch off a financed phone if the customer falls behind on payments.
Why M-KOPA bought KilpiTek
M-KOPA’s model works like this: you pay a small deposit, take the phone home, then pay daily or weekly until you own it. Banks normally ask for collateral before lending. For phone sellers, the phone itself is the security, and that only works if it can be locked remotely.
M-KOPA said the deal was meant to “bring in-house a critical device-locking capability” and strengthen control over a key part of its technology platform. It also expects the move to help its phone sourcing strategy.
The Kenyan startup is known to operate pay-as-you-go phone financing across multiple African markets. Owning KilpiTek means it no longer depends on an outside supplier for that locking function.
What this means for you in Ghana
If you buy a phone on a pay-as-you-go plan, the lock is the reason you can walk out of the shop without paying the full price upfront. If that lock fails or gets too expensive to run, the plans get pricier or disappear.
Bringing the technology in-house could make M-KOPA’s repayment system more reliable. That matters because a sudden lock on your phone when you are behind on payments is already part of how these plans work.
It is also a reminder: a financed phone is not fully yours until you finish paying. Miss enough instalments and the device can be restricted, no matter which brand or shop you used.
What to watch
Watch how M-KOPA prices its phone plans in Ghana over the coming months. If owning its own locking software cuts costs, that saving may or may not reach customers. Also check the repayment terms before you sign up: know the daily amount, the total cost, and exactly what happens if you miss a payment.

articles.title: S. Korea officially launches FTA push with Egypt, its first in North Africa - 헤럴드경제
articles.summary: S. Korea officially launches FTA push with Egypt, its first in North Africa  헤럴드경제
articles.full_text:
South Korea has officially launched free trade agreement negotiations with Egypt, marking the first such push with a North African country. The two sides also agreed to pursue cooperation in eco-friendly shipbuilding infrastructure in line with Egypt's "2030 Suez Canal Green Strategy."
The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said Thursday that Park Jung-sung, South Korea's chief trade negotiator, and Egyptian Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid Saleh signed a joint declaration to launch Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) negotiations during a bilateral summit held on the occasion of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's state visit to South Korea. The ministry said the declaration carries particular significance as it marks the first time South Korea has launched CEPA negotiations with a North African country.
The two leaders had earlier agreed to actively pursue CEPA discussions during a summit held when President Lee Jae Myung made an official visit to Egypt in November last year.
A CEPA is a trade agreement that offers greater flexibility in structure and level of market opening than a conventional free trade agreement, while strengthening cooperation across a broad range of sectors.
Egypt is Africa's second-largest economy and a key hub in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, with high growth potential underpinned by a population of about 120 million.
Park held separate meetings Thursday with Egypt's minister of investment and foreign trade, minister of industry, and head of the Suez Canal Economic Zone Authority to discuss follow-up cooperation aimed at translating the economic momentum from the summit into concrete outcomes.
The two sides agreed to broaden cooperation across multiple areas, including laying the groundwork for expanded bilateral trade and investment through early CEPA negotiations, reviewing the status of South Korean companies' major operations in Egypt such as home appliances and apparel, and resolving business difficulties to facilitate corporate activity and investment.
Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan also signed a memorandum of understanding on shipbuilding cooperation with his Egyptian counterpart, Industry Minister Khaled Hashem, aimed at strengthening the two countries' shipbuilding capabilities and supporting the sector's green transition.
The ministry said it expects South Korean shipbuilders to expand their presence in the Egyptian market through future cooperation on next-generation vessel construction and repair, specialty ship building, and equipment exports, combining South Korea's world-class shipbuilding technology with Egypt's commitment to developing its own shipbuilding industry.

articles.title: Hedging by Design: Southeast Asia's Engagement with BRICS - orfonline.org
articles.summary: Hedging by Design: Southeast Asia's Engagement with BRICS  orfonline.org
articles.full_text:
Southeast Asian countries are engaging with BRICS to widen their economic and diplomatic options, using it as a hedging platform in preference to exclusive alignment with any major power
Image Source:  Getty Images 
The BRICS summit, held on 12–13 September 2026 in New Delhi, brought together non-Western leaders to discuss the future of the global economy and development challenges. Leaders from Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and the Philippines, all major members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), also attended. Although part of routine diplomacy, their visit coincided with major shifts in global geopolitics and the international economy, raising the grouping's importance for them. Each ASEAN member, however, has its own reason for participating. This article examines the drivers of Southeast Asian participation in BRICS and how perceptions of the grouping are shifting in the region as global headwinds intensify.
Southeast Asia's engagement with BRICS reflects the region's increasingly differentiated approach to a shifting global order. Indonesia became a full BRICS member in 2025. In contrast, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam are BRICS partner countries, a status that connects them to the grouping without the privileges of full membership. The Philippines has also engaged with the grouping as part of its broader economic and diplomatic outreach.
As the region's largest economy and the world's leading nickel producer, Indonesia sees BRICS as an avenue to pursue its downstream industrial ambitions, particularly in electric vehicle (EV) supply chains, and to strengthen its long-standing campaign for greater Global South representation. Other ASEAN members have taken different approaches, although economic diversification remains a common consideration. Malaysia, for instance, has sought to use its BRICS partnership to diversify its economic relations and support global governance reforms, while maintaining extensive ties with Western and Asian markets. Thailand, meanwhile, views BRICS as a means to expand its markets and consolidate its position as a regional economic and connectivity hub.
Vietnam has adopted a more cautious approach, reflecting its deep integration into Western-led trade networks and its preference for a balanced external posture. The Philippines, meanwhile, has tied its BRICS engagement to broader regional priorities, including supply-chain resilience and economic connectivity. These approaches show that Southeast Asian engagement with BRICS is driven by country-specific economic and foreign-policy interests rather than a single strategic objective.
Beyond its geopolitical heft, BRICS gives Southeast Asian countries a platform to shape global discourse and developments on major issues, including conflicts, trade, global governance, and norms around critical and emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI).
At the same time, ASEAN members that remain outside the BRICS framework could potentially face disadvantages if the grouping develops preferential financing mechanisms, trade arrangements or other forms of institutionalised economic cooperation. This gives Southeast Asian members a further reason to stay engaged with BRICS, even if full membership is not an immediate objective.
Beyond its geopolitical heft, BRICS gives Southeast Asian countries a platform to shape global discourse and developments on major issues, including conflicts, trade, global governance, and norms around critical and emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI). While ASEAN remains largely focused on regional issues, particularly trade, BRICS provides greater opportunities for Southeast Asian countries to participate in global conversations. Furthermore, the grouping is increasingly seen as a more legitimate representative of the Global South, given the presence of developing countries and emerging economies. No other grouping, except the Group of Seven (G7), has comparable standing today.
The growing interest in BRICS can also be understood through the lens of hedging. Rather than choosing between competing geopolitical camps, Southeast Asian countries seek to maximise strategic autonomy by maintaining relationships with multiple major powers. A South-South platform is increasingly relevant as geopolitical rivalry spills into trade, technology, investment, and supply chains.
For Southeast Asian economies, the economic dimension is particularly important. BRICS brings together some of the world's largest emerging economies, which together account for 40 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP) and 26 percent of global trade. This provides access to expanding markets, investment opportunities, and alternative channels of financial cooperation. The grouping's emphasis on local-currency transactions and greater representation for developing countries in global institutions also resonates with ASEAN's long-standing preference for a more inclusive and multipolar economic order.
The idea is not to view BRICS as a substitute for established ties with Western economies. Relationships with the United States, the European Union, Japan and other partners in trade, investment, security and technology remain significant.
BRICS is useful precisely because it does not require an exclusive alignment. By engaging the grouping, ASEAN members can signal that their foreign-policy options are not confined to a US-China binary. The partner country format allows ASEAN members to engage without being tied to its official position. At the same time, participation allows them to strengthen ties with China, India, Russia and other established and emerging powers without necessarily endorsing their strategic positions. The appeal of BRICS, therefore, lies less in collective bloc-building than in expanding the diplomatic and economic space available to individual Southeast Asian states. As global headwinds intensify, such flexibility is likely to become an increasingly valuable component of ASEAN’s broader hedging strategy.
The participation of diverse regional groupings, represented by their chairs at the summit, makes BRICS more representative of the world. These include the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), ASEAN, the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC), the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), the African Union (AU), and the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC). Their participation brings to the fore issues that remain on the periphery of global governance. The Philippines' participation as ASEAN chair, despite its status as a US treaty ally, underscores BRICS’ importance for economic diplomacy.
Although it remains focused on global issues, BRICS has emerged as a vital platform for deepening economic and trade cooperation and strengthening investment channels between its members and those of these regional groupings. Although BRICS may not hold a unified position on security matters, unlike the G7, its support for economic cooperation gives it more weight today than many other forums, including the G7 and the Group of Twenty (G20). As the global economy comes under strain, the grouping's strategic profile will continue to grow, advancing economic and trade cooperation alongside its original focus on global governance and multilateralism.
ASEAN members' differing approaches reflect a preference for strategic flexibility over exclusive alignment. How this engagement evolves will depend on BRICS’ institutional development, its compatibility with countries’ strategic interests, and its relationship with ASEAN’s centrality and existing regional frameworks.
Southeast Asian countries' connection with BRICS is recent, dating from the introduction of the partner-country category at the 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan, held under Russia's chairship in October 2024. Since then, interest in deeper engagement has grown, although the extent to which individual Southeast Asian countries seek full membership varies. A fragmenting global order, weakening multilateralism, weak global governance, and intensifying great-power politics have contributed to BRICS' appeal among Southeast Asian countries.
However, the grouping faces challenges, including rival blocs and the absence of a common agenda. Nonetheless, despite these obstacles, interest remains, underscoring its strategic importance. Lastly, this interest will likely continue to grow.

articles.full_text:
The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) has once again received international recognition for its strategic communication and stakeholder engagement efforts, with the Comptroller-General of Customs, Adewale Adeniyi, receiving a Special Award of Excellence at the 2026 International Public Relations Association (IPRA) Golden World Awards in Athens, Greece, on Friday, 25 September 2026.
The award recognises the Service’s approach to transparent communication, stakeholder engagement and ethical public relations in supporting the implementation and public understanding of its ongoing reforms, particularly initiatives aimed at modernising Customs operations, improving trade facilitation and strengthening institutional transparency.
Receiving the recognition, CGC Adeniyi described the honour as international acknowledgement of the Nigeria Customs Service’s reform efforts, noting that it would further encourage the Service to deepen its adoption of emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, in public communication and stakeholder engagement.
“We have started using AI tools in our public communication, and we view this recognition as an invitation to do more. By 2027, we hope the NCS and more Nigerian agencies will feature prominently among global award recipients,” he said.
CGC Adeniyi said effective communication remained critical to the success of government reforms because citizens and stakeholders needed to understand their objectives, implementation challenges and expected benefits. He added that the NCS reform agenda aligns with President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s economic policies, particularly efforts to improve Nigeria’s trade competitiveness, facilitate exports, and strengthen the country’s participation in the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).
He further celebrated Nigeria’s win at the IPRA Grand Prix, describing the achievement as an indication of the country’s growing participation in international strategic communication. The Grand Prix was awarded to Image Merchants Promotion Limited (IMPR), publishers of PRNigeria and Economic Confidential, for its campaign, AI for Crisis Communication: From Study to Strategy.
The campaign grew out of a research project led by IMPR’s Chief Executive Officer, Yushau Shuaib, in collaboration with the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) and the Centre for Crisis Communication.
Earlier in her welcome remarks, the President of the International Public Relations Association (IPRA), Esther Cobbah, stated that the return to Athens was particularly significant because the city was where the association developed its Code of Conduct for public relations practice 60 years ago.

Oduwole Lists FMITI’s Contributions Toward Attaining Nigeria’s Aspiration for $1trn Economy
Dike Onwuamaeze
The Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment’s (FMITI) implementation of Nigeria’s quest to attain a $1trillion economy by 2030 has increased the country’s capital importation from $3.91 billion in 2023 to $23.22 billion in 2025 and increased foreign direct investments inflow to Nigeria to $.92 billion in 2025 from $.38 billion and $.68 billion in 2023 and 2024 respectively.
These figures were disclosed in a presentation to the Economic Management Team by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment Dr. Jumoke Oduwole, on October 6.
The presentation was titled, “Industry, Trade and Investment: Our Contribution to the $1 Trillion Economy.”
According to the presentation, the non-oil share of Nigeria’s export earnings grew from 11.7 per cent in 2024 to 14.5 per cent in 2025.
It stated that Nigeria recorded N12.36 trillion non-oil export revenue in 2025 across over 120 countries as well as 21 per cent increase in Nigeria’s intra-African trade in 2025 and 500 per cent increase in Certificates of Origin issued in 2025.
Other milestones recorded by the FMITI under the leadership of Oduwole were 40.6 per cent increase in the quantity of vehicles assembled in Nigeria in 2025 and 474.74 per cent increase in cassava starch production in 2025.
The country also recorded 16.67 per cent increase in light electronics production in 2025, achieved 24,668 tonnes traded volume on the Nigeria Commodity Exchange (NCX), in 2025 up from 3,942 tonnes and N4 billion traded value on the NCX in the same period up from N1.9 billion.
In addition, 96,035 documents were processed in the National Single Window between March and July 2026.
The minister of FMITI said that the ministry’s strategic direction is to, “Unlock global and regional demand to drive non-oil exports and industrial productivity at scale; strengthen domestic industrial capacity and productivity for the supply of export-ready goods and services; mobilise strategic and inclusive investment for productive infrastructure, innovation, and industrial transformation as well as leveraging data, AI, digital infrastructure and strategic communication to enable target.”
She stated that productive investments in the country’s economy have helped existing businesses to expand and convert credible projects into operating capacity.
According to her, the ministry’s strategic direction has also helped non-oil exporters to, “reach buyers, meet standards and use market-access opportunities and improved the price, quality and availability of Nigerian goods to serve domestic demand.”
Oduwole said that progress achieved in the implementation of strategies to achieve the $1 trillion economy included modernisation of regulatory architecture through, “advanced modernisation of investment rules and institutions to attract quality investment.”
She noted that bilateral investment frameworks have strengthened government-to-government support through frameworks such as US CIP, UK ETIP and UAE CEPA.
The minister added that under the centralised coordination of investment engagements, the FMITI will engage all ministries and state governments for centralised coordination of bilateral MoUs and investment agreements that are above an agreed value threshold, with support from Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Justice.
She stated that the FMITI will, “maintain a central register, clear delivery responsibilities and consistent reporting to strengthen MoU discipline and government credibility. And coordinate implementation, improve investor awareness and access, and track uptake and investment outcomes.”
The minister stated that the FMITI is enhancing the industrial production base, adding that economic wins so far include the achievement of real growth by manufacturing sub-sectors Q1
2026 as cement, pharmaceuticals, automotive assembly recorded 11.53, 6.15 and 5.44 growth rate respectively while the Food, Beverage and Tobacco recorded 4.10 in Q1 of 2026.
According to Oduwole, the FMITI is fast-tracking the implementation of the Nigeria First Policy and Nigeria Industrial Policy; scaling MSME and large enterprise financing through Bank of Industry and Nigeria Export and Import Bank and is also pursuing, “coordinated evidence-based tariff review,” and balancing fiscal, trade and industrial policy.
